questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A flat gradient is not a right answer
questions.learningObjective: explain why a small gradient certifies a stopping point and not a good fit
questions.stem: Explain why a run that stops as soon as its gradient falls below 0.01 cannot claim the model is right, and give the sentence that gets this wrong.

answer.exemplar: A gradient is a local quantity: it says which way the loss would move if the parameters moved a little in every direction at once, and nothing about how far the parameters are from a good place. The threshold is reached when the loss surface is flat in the directions the parameters can move, which happens at a minimum, at a saddle, and at a plateau, and it also happens early on a shallow surface where the parameters are nowhere near right. On a single parameter with curvature two and a step of 0.1, the gradient falls below 0.01 after 35 updates, at which point the parameter is 0.0048677783 and the loss is of the order of 1e-5, yet the same threshold on a surface ten times flatter would be crossed at a parameter ten times further from its optimum, with a loss a hundred times larger. The sentence that gets this wrong is the one that says the parameters were correct to within 0.01, because 0.01 is a bound on a slope and has no units of parameter at all: it is reported in the units of the loss, and dividing a loss by a distance gives a slope, not an error. The related wrong sentence claims that a vanishing gradient means the model has converged on the right answer, which confuses the search finishing with the search being right, and a third claims the loss must be zero at such a point, which is false whenever the response carries noise the model cannot predict.

questions.explanation: The value of the threshold is that it is cheap and it is a statement about the optimiser, not about the model. A gradient is a ratio of change in loss to change in parameters, so bounding it bounds a slope; the distance from the optimum is a different quantity and the two are related only through the curvature of the loss between the current point and the optimum. Where the surface is steep, a small gradient means the parameters are close; where it is shallow, the same small gradient is consistent with being far away. The other thing the threshold cannot see is which stationary point was reached, since a saddle and a minimum are indistinguishable to a first-order test, and that is the reason a restart with a different seed is a genuine check rather than superstition. The disciplined practice is to treat the gradient threshold as a stopping rule, to judge the model on held-out data, and to report the held-out figure as the performance claim.
questions.hint: Ask what a gradient is a ratio of, and what that makes a bound on it a bound on.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a decaying step size buys and cannot fix
questions.learningObjective: state what a learning-rate schedule changes and what it leaves broken
questions.stem: Explain what a step size that starts at 0.1 and falls by half its excess each pass buys a run, and name the fault it cannot repair.

answer.exemplar: A schedule buys two things and neither is a repair. The first is the stability that a fixed step size cannot give: on a loss whose curvature grows as the run moves into a steeper region, one step size cannot be right everywhere, and a decaying one is right near the start. The second is the quiet settling that a fixed step size cannot give either, because a constant step keeps bouncing around the minimum with an amplitude set by the step, so the parameters never stop moving and the reported loss keeps carrying a variance that has nothing to do with the data. With an exponential schedule at 0.1 and a rate of 0.5 the step falls to 0.0135335 by the fourth pass and below 0.01 at the fifth, which is what turns a descent into a settle. What it cannot repair is a step size that was too large to begin with: the schedule starts from the starting value, so if that value is past the stability limit of the loss the first updates are the ones that damage the run, and decaying from there shrinks the damage rather than removing it, which is why the schedule has to begin at a value the loss tolerates. The sentence that gets this wrong is the one that says adding a schedule fixed the run, because a schedule changes the size of the steps rather than the direction they point, and a badly chosen direction is untouched by it. A related wrong sentence claims a schedule can rescue a diverging run, which confuses a decaying multiplier with a sign change: a positive multiplier never turns a descent into an ascent, and a run that needs that needs a smaller first step, not a smaller hundredth step.

questions.explanation: The mechanism is the multiplier each update applies, and everything a schedule does follows from how that multiplier changes. A fixed step size on a quadratic is a fixed multiplier, so the parameters approach the minimum geometrically and then oscillate around it forever with an amplitude set by the step; shrinking the step shrinks that amplitude and eventually makes the oscillation invisible at the precision the loss is reported to. The limit of the mechanism is equally clear. The schedule multiplies the step by a number between zero and one and never changes its sign, so it can damp an overshooting descent but cannot reverse a direction that is wrong, and it cannot rescue a first step that was already past the stability limit, because the damage is done before the schedule has had a chance to act. That is why the starting value is a decision in its own right and why a schedule is usually paired with a search over the starting value rather than substituted for one.
questions.hint: Ask what the schedule multiplies, and whether that multiplier can change a direction or only a size.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The same penalty written on two different loss scales
questions.learningObjective: explain why a penalty strength only means something relative to the loss it is added to
questions.stem: Explain why a penalty strength quoted without saying whether the loss is a sum over rows or a mean over rows cannot be reproduced, using coefficients 1.5, -2.0 and 0.5, a strength of 0.3 and a training set of 320 rows whose summed squared error is 16.0.

answer.exemplar: A penalty is a number, and a strength is a ratio between that number and a loss, so the loss's units are part of the strength's meaning. With coefficients 1.5, -2.0 and 0.5 the sum of the squares is 6.5 and a strength of 0.3 adds 1.95 to the objective. Added to a summed loss, where the data term is 16.0, the objective becomes 17.95 and the penalty is 10.86 per cent of it. Added to a mean loss, where the data term is 16.0 over 320 rows, which is 0.05, the same penalty makes the objective 2.0 and the penalty is 97.5 per cent of it, which is not regularisation at all but a decision to ignore the data. To keep the same proportion on a mean basis the strength would have to rise from 0.3 to 39.0, a factor of 130, because the two losses differ by the row count. The sentence that gets this wrong is the one that reports a strength of 0.3 and calls it mild, because mild and severe are the same words for the two conventions and the report does not say which is in force. A related wrong sentence says the convention is a matter of presentation, which it is not: a fitting loop that sums the loss and takes a step of a fixed size is descending a surface 320 times steeper than one that averages, and the same step size that is stable on the second diverges on the first.

questions.explanation: This is the same reason a step size needs a scale, arriving from the other end. The data term and the penalty term are only comparable if they are in the same units, and the row count is exactly the factor that separates a summed loss from a mean one, so a strength quoted without that convention is a strength quoted without its denominator. The arithmetic above is the demonstration: the penalty's share of the objective is 10.86 per cent on a summed basis and 97.5 per cent on a mean basis, and holding the share fixed needs a factor of 130 in the strength, which is 320 rows against a data term of 16.0. Two practical consequences follow. A strength tuned under one convention and applied under the other changes the model's behaviour by two orders of magnitude, which is why configurations are stored with the convention attached. And a mean-basis loss is usually the better default, because it makes a strength comparable across datasets of different sizes, which is the property a team actually wants when a penalty is moved from one table to another.
questions.hint: Ask what the penalty's share of the objective is under each convention, and what factor of strength separates them.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The order in which a regulariser earns its place
questions.learningObjective: order the steps that take an overfitting run to a defensible model
questions.stem: A run's training loss falls from 0.61 to 0.09 over six passes while its validation loss bottoms at 0.53 on the third pass and rises to 0.62. Put these four steps in the order that produces a model someone can defend.

options.text: Confirm the diagnosis on the two loss curves before changing anything, since a rising validation loss is the evidence the whole plan rests on
Add a penalty and re-run, since a constraint on the coefficients is the cheapest way to buy back the variance the later passes spent
Report the held-out figure from data that took no part in choosing the pass, since a minimum over six validation figures is smaller than any one of them
Keep the checkpoint from the third pass, since it is free and the passes after it made the model worse on the only data that was held out

questions.explanation: The diagnosis precedes the change, the free change precedes the costly one, and the reporting rule is settled before any figure is quoted. Reading the two curves first is not ceremony: the whole plan assumes the fit has too much freedom for the data behind it, and the alternative diagnosis, a model that cannot fit its own rows, would call for capacity rather than a penalty, so the order of the first two steps decides which of the remaining steps is even relevant. Taking the third-pass checkpoint comes next because it costs nothing and already delivers most of the benefit, and a team that refits before trying it has added a day of work to a problem it had not yet solved. The penalty then buys back the variance more durably, and it is a change worth making only because the diagnosis was made. The reporting rule is fixed last but applies to every number in the report, because the quoted figure has to come from rows that did not choose the pass, and a minimum over six validation figures is optimistically biased by exactly the selection that produced it.
questions.hint: Sequence by what has to be known, then by what costs least, and settle how results will be quoted before quoting any.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A model that fits the rows it was given
questions.learningObjective: name the fault a falling training loss with a rising validation loss describes and its remedies
questions.stem: A run's training loss falls monotonically from 0.61 to 0.09 across six passes while its validation loss falls to 0.53 and then climbs to 0.62, and the team proposes to add hidden units. Which reading and which response belong together?

options.text: The fit is short of capacity, and the response is to double the hidden width, since a training loss that has reached 0.09 must have run out of parameters
options.misconception: reads a low training loss as a shortage of capacity rather than as freedom being spent

options.text: The data is wrong, and the response is to re-check the validation set, since a validation loss that rises while the training loss falls points at a mismatch between the two tables
options.misconception: attributes a growing gap to a mismatch between two tables rather than to the fit

options.text: The fit has too much freedom for its data, and the response is a constraint of some kind: a penalty, fewer units, or a stop at the third pass, with the reported figure taken from rows that chose nothing
The fit has too much freedom for its data, and the response is to add hidden units so the network can reach the true function underneath the noise
options.misconception: pairs the right diagnosis with the one change that grants the fit more freedom

questions.explanation: The gap between the two curves is the diagnosis and the sign of the change follows from it. Validation minus training runs from minus 0.02 at the first pass to 0.53 at the sixth, the validation loss reaches its low of 0.53 at the third pass and then rises by 0.09 while the training loss falls by 0.27 over the same three passes, which is the ordinary signature of a fit absorbing noise. The remedies are all constraints of the same kind, differing in where they are applied: a penalty constrains the coefficients, fewer units constrain the architecture, and stopping at the third pass constrains how long the fit is allowed to run. Adding units is the one move that makes the fault worse, because it grants the fit more freedom at the moment the evidence says it already has too much. The capacity reading is a direct inversion, since a training loss of 0.09 is low rather than high and a model unable to fit its own rows is the opposite condition. The data reading is a reasonable worry in general, since a validation table built from a different population would produce exactly this picture, and it is worth a check, but it is a different diagnosis with a different fix and it should be raised as its own question rather than folded into this one.
questions.hint: Read the gap between the curves and ask whether the fit needs more room or less.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a run cannot claim from a loss on its own rows
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a fit's own loss from evidence that it will generalise
questions.stem: A report states that the final training loss of 0.09 is a measure of how well the model has learned, and a second report states that the same model will achieve 0.09 on future data. Explain what the first statement supports and why the second does not follow.

answer.exemplar: A loss on the rows a model was fitted to measures how well the fit absorbed those particular rows, which is a statement about the optimisation and not about the model. It is low for two very different reasons: the model found structure that generalises, or the model has enough freedom to reproduce the particular values it was shown, including their noise, and the training loss cannot tell those apart. In this run the distinction is visible rather than theoretical, because the loss on the held-out rows bottoms at 0.53 on the third pass and rises to 0.62 while the training loss keeps falling to 0.09, so the last three passes bought 0.27 of training loss and 0.09 of validation loss. The second statement is therefore contradicted by the run's own second curve. The sentence that gets it wrong is the one that says the training loss shows how well the model has learned, because the word learned is the load-bearing one: the run's own held-out figure is 0.62 at the pass where the training figure is 0.09, a gap of 0.53, and a model that had learned the pattern would not show a gap that grows. A related wrong sentence treats a low training loss as evidence of a good model on the grounds that a model that cannot fit its own rows is certainly worse, which confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one: fitting the rows is necessary and tells you nothing on its own about what happens to rows the fit has not seen.

questions.explanation: The distinction is between a quantity the optimiser can drive down and a quantity the data has to grant. Training loss belongs to the first category, which is why it is a useful optimisation signal and a useless performance claim. Held-out loss belongs to the second, and the gap between them is the only thing that speaks to generalisation, because it is the difference between what the model absorbed and what it can reproduce. Two related habits keep this honest. The held-out figure used to choose a pass, a penalty or a step size stops being held-out for that purpose, so the performance claim needs a third set of rows that took part in nothing, which is the same reason a holdout is read once. And the gap is itself worth watching over a run: a gap that grows while the training loss falls is the earliest available warning that the extra passes are being spent on noise, and it appears several passes before the held-out loss itself turns upward.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two numbers the optimiser could have driven down on its own, and what the gap between them means.
